sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle3\cos t, 3\sin t\rangle$. Find $\vec{v}(t)$, $\vec{a}(t)$, and verify that $\vec{a}(t)$ points toward the origin (is a scalar multiple of $-\vec{r}(t)$).
questions.target: Motion on a circle and centripetal acceleration
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle-3\sin t,3\cos t\rangle$. $\vec{a}(t)=\langle-3\cos t,-3\sin t\rangle=-\vec{r}(t)$. Since $\vec{a}(t)$ is exactly $-1$ times $\vec{r}(t)$, it points directly toward the origin (centripetal acceleration).
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle-3\sin t,3\cos t\rangle$. $\vec{a}(t)=\langle-3\cos t,-3\sin t\rangle=-\vec{r}(t)$. Since $\vec{a}(t)$ is exactly $-1$ times $\vec{r}(t)$, it points directly toward the origin (centripetal acceleration).

questions.q: A projectile is launched with position $\vec{r}(t)=\langle 20t, 30t-4.9t^2\rangle$ (meters, seconds). Find the velocity vector $\vec{v}(t)$ and the time when the projectile reaches maximum height (where the vertical velocity component is $0$).
questions.target: Projectile motion as a vector-valued function
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle20,30-9.8t\rangle$. Maximum height occurs when $30-9.8t=0 \Rightarrow t=\frac{30}{9.8}\approx3.06$ s.
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle20,30-9.8t\rangle$. Maximum height occurs when $30-9.8t=0 \Rightarrow t=\frac{30}{9.8}\approx3.06$ s.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: For the particle above, find the magnitude of the acceleration vector at $t=0$.
For $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t,t^2\rangle$, find the unit tangent vector $\vec{T}(t)$ at $t=1$.
Explain why $\vec{T}(t)=\frac{\vec{v}(t)}{|\vec{v}(t)|}$ always has magnitude $1$.
questions.answer: Dividing any nonzero vector by its own magnitude produces a vector with magnitude $\frac{|\vec{v}(t)|}{|\vec{v}(t)|}=1$ by definition — this is the standard construction of a unit vector in the same direction.
questions.explanation: Dividing any nonzero vector by its own magnitude produces a vector with magnitude $\frac{|\vec{v}(t)|}{|\vec{v}(t)|}=1$ by definition — this is the standard construction of a unit vector in the same direction.

questions.q: For the same particle, verify that $\vec{v}(t)\cdot\vec{r}(t)=0$ for all $t$, and interpret this geometrically.
questions.target: Motion on a circle and centripetal acceleration
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)\cdot\vec{r}(t)=(-3\sin t)(3\cos t)+(3\cos t)(3\sin t)=-9\sin t\cos t+9\sin t\cos t=0$. This confirms the velocity vector is always perpendicular to the position vector — consistent with circular motion, where velocity is tangent to the circle.
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(t)\cdot\vec{r}(t)=(-3\sin t)(3\cos t)+(3\cos t)(3\sin t)=-9\sin t\cos t+9\sin t\cos t=0$. This confirms the velocity vector is always perpendicular to the position vector — consistent with circular motion, where velocity is tangent to the circle.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Find the dot product $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w}$ for $\vec{u}=\langle3,-2\rangle$ and $\vec{w}=\langle-1,4\rangle$, and state whether the vectors are perpendicular.
questions.cross_lesson: 6.01 Power Series and Interval of Convergence
questions.answer: $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w}=3(-1)+(-2)(4)=-3-8=-11$. Since the dot product is not $0$, the vectors are NOT perpendicular.
questions.explanation: $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{w}=3(-1)+(-2)(4)=-3-8=-11$. Since the dot product is not $0$, the vectors are NOT perpendicular.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3,t^2\rangle$. Find the times $t$ when the particle's speed is exactly $\sqrt{13}$.
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2,2t\rangle$. Speed$^2=9t^4+4t^2=13$. Let $w=t^2$: $9w^2+4w-13=0$. Using the quadratic formula: $w=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{16+468}}{18}=\frac{-4\pm22}{18}$. Taking the positive root: $w=1$, so $t^2=1 \Rightarrow t=\pm1$.
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2,2t\rangle$. Speed$^2=9t^4+4t^2=13$. Let $w=t^2$: $9w^2+4w-13=0$. Using the quadratic formula: $w=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{16+468}}{18}=\frac{-4\pm22}{18}$. Taking the positive root: $w=1$, so $t^2=1 \Rightarrow t=\pm1$.

questions.q: For the particle $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t,\ln t\rangle$ ($t>0$), find the velocity vector and speed at $t=1$.
For the same projectile, find the speed at $t=0$ (launch) and interpret its two components.
questions.target: Projectile motion as a vector-valued function
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(0)=\langle20,30\rangle$. Speed $=\sqrt{20^2+30^2}=\sqrt{400+900}=\sqrt{1300}\approx36.1$ m/s. The horizontal component ($20$ m/s) stays constant throughout the flight, while the vertical component ($30$ m/s initially) decreases due to gravity.
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(0)=\langle20,30\rangle$. Speed $=\sqrt{20^2+30^2}=\sqrt{400+900}=\sqrt{1300}\approx36.1$ m/s. The horizontal component ($20$ m/s) stays constant throughout the flight, while the vertical component ($30$ m/s initially) decreases due to gravity.

questions.q: A particle moves along $\vec{r}(t)=\langle t^3-3t,\, t^2-4\rangle$. Find all times $t$ when the particle is momentarily at rest (both velocity components equal $0$ simultaneously).
questions.target: Finding when a particle is at rest
questions.answer: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-3,2t\rangle$. Need $3t^2-3=0$ AND $2t=0$ simultaneously. From the second equation, $t=0$; check the first: $3(0)^2-3=-3\neq0$. There is NO time when both components are zero at once, so the particle is never fully at rest.
questions.explanation: $\vec{v}(t)=\langle3t^2-3,2t\rangle$. Need $3t^2-3=0$ AND $2t=0$ simultaneously. From the second equation, $t=0$; check the first: $3(0)^2-3=-3\neq0$. There is NO time when both components are zero at once, so the particle is never fully at rest.

questions.q: Write an integral for the total distance traveled by a particle from $t = 0$ to $t = 5$ with $\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle \cos(t^2), e^{\sqrt{t}} \rangle$.
questions.answer: Distance traveled is $\int_0^5 ||\mathbf{v}(t)|| dt = \int_0^5 \sqrt{(\cos(t^2))^2 + (e^{\sqrt{t}})^2} dt = \int_0^5 \sqrt{\cos^2(t^2) + e^{2\sqrt{t}}} dt$.
questions.explanation: Distance traveled is $\int_0^5 ||\mathbf{v}(t)|| dt = \int_0^5 \sqrt{(\cos(t^2))^2 + (e^{\sqrt{t}})^2} dt = \int_0^5 \sqrt{\cos^2(t^2) + e^{2\sqrt{t}}} dt$.
questions.cross_lesson: 6.01 Power Series and Interval of Convergence
